analysis.title: On Our Minds: 2026 Midterms Postmortem: A Blue Wave
key_insights: Democrats won the 2026 midterms comfortably: at least 54 Senate seats and more than 235 House seats, with two Senate races (Alaska, Mississippi) and several dozen House races still uncalled.

SG's final Senate model predicted about 51-52 Democratic seats, so the result beat the model and polls. The final model run had signaled a higher likelihood of an above-52 outcome than the prior week.
Affordability was the central voter concern. Republicans lost key red-state races in South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Iowa, and Texas elected a Democratic governor.
Policy uncertainty rises under divided government. Democrats could demand reversals of One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBBA) provisions in debt ceiling negotiations.
SG expects no new major legislation, because of the Senate filibuster and the presidential veto. It expects more House oversight hearings and subpoenas of CEOs and administration officials.
The administration is expected to lean on areas where the executive has most power relative to Congress, such as foreign policy and tariffs.

Republican divisions are visible. Some Republicans questioned Trump's hand-picked candidates in deep-red states. JD Vance's post blamed the Iran war, the affordability crisis and the US relationship with Israel. SG says this may relate to a possible 2028 campaign.

AI is the main driver of recent US growth. SG expects no immediate impact on AI development from the Democratic win, but more hearings for industry leaders. Voter concern over local data center buildouts contributed to Democratic governor wins in deep-red states such as Texas.
State-level policy remains hard to pass where the legislature and governor are split between parties. State legislature outcomes in many contested states are still to be determined.
Historically, primary deficits as a share of potential GDP become less loose when the President's party loses the House. SG already assumed a House loss in its 2026-2027 GDP outlook.
SG's 2026 fiscal impulse is a one-off. It comes from larger tax refunds and OBBBA and fades going into 2027, since a House loss removes discretionary fiscal policy for the rest of the term.

SG forecasts 2026 GDP growth at 2.6% Q4/Q4, above trend, with second-round effects keeping consumption and business investment elevated in 2H. It expects growth to slow by end-2026 as the fiscal impulse wanes and the Fed gradually tightens.
SG forecasts 2027 GDP growth at 1.7% Q4/Q4, just below its 1.8% trend estimate, with growth below trend in 1H 2027.
SG's overall call is gridlock. The Democratic majorities are too small to override the filibuster or a veto, and the Democratic win was larger than SG expected.

macro_indicators.interpretation: SG expects gradual Fed tightening to add to slowing growth as the fiscal impulse wanes.

risk_factors: Policy uncertainty from divided government, including debt ceiling negotiations in which Democrats could demand OBBBA reversals.
House oversight hearings and subpoenas of CEOs and administration officials, including AI industry leaders.
Fiscal impulse fades in 2027, with GDP growth slowing below trend in 1H 2027.
Gradual Fed tightening alongside the fading fiscal impulse.
Further executive action on tariffs and foreign policy, where Congress has limited ability to constrain the administration.
Split party control at the state level can block state policy, with state legislature outcomes still to be determined.
geopolitical: Republican figures, including JD Vance, cited the Iran war and the US relationship with Israel as reasons for the Republican midterm losses.
SG expects the administration to focus on foreign policy and tariffs, where the executive has more power relative to Congress.
